note: Canonical Writing Model — domain-specific pedagogical knowledge, loaded as DATA by the domain-independent Developmental Guide Engine. These are culturally established FUNCTIONS of effective writing and cultural RESOURCES the engine uses to interpret student writing. They are NOT developmental stages, NOT a required instructional sequence, and NOT rigid templates. The engine must decide which domains are currently relevant; it must never force students through the domains in a predetermined order.

domains.governing_communicative_function: Prepare a reader to enter the essay's developing world of meaning — help the reader understand enough of the subject, situation, question, problem, experience, or argument to follow what comes next. The exact work required depends on the essay's purpose and genre.
communicative_functions: prepare or state a central claim
indicate the direction of the essay
possible_communicative_functions: distinguish the specific focus from the broader topic
establish common ground with the reader
introduce a tension, contradiction, puzzle, or uncertainty
indicate the direction of the essay
establish the relationship between writer and audience
create expectations appropriate to the genre
domains.engine_note_on_functions: Do not assume that every opening needs to perform every function.
reader_needs: knowing what the essay is about
knowing which part of a broad topic matters
understanding the immediate context
understanding why the topic matters
understanding the problem or question
knowing what is at stake
understanding unfamiliar terms
knowing whose perspective is being represented
understanding why the writer is addressing the issue
knowing what kind of essay is beginning
receiving enough orientation to interpret the next paragraph
being given a reason to continue reading
domains.reader_needs_note: These are interpretive possibilities, not mandatory requirements.
domains.resources_note: Introduce a resource only when it serves the student's operative purpose and the needs of the reader. No resource is automatically required.

observable_organizations.name: Topic naming
observable_organizations.description: Identifies a general subject but has not yet differentiated a specific focus, problem, question, or purpose.
observable_organizations.example: Social media is an important part of life today.

observable_organizations.name: Topic plus context
observable_organizations.description: Identifies a subject and supplies background, but the reader may not yet know why the subject matters.

observable_organizations.name: Topic plus position
observable_organizations.description: States an opinion or claim quickly, but the conceptual context or significance may remain unclear.

observable_organizations.name: Situation without explicit purpose
observable_organizations.description: Creates a scene, anecdote, or example, but its relationship to the essay's larger purpose is not yet visible.

observable_organizations.name: Problem framing
observable_organizations.description: Identifies a conflict, tension, difficulty, or unresolved issue that organizes the opening.

observable_organizations.name: Question framing
observable_organizations.description: Organizes the opening around a question or puzzle.

observable_organizations.name: Significance framing
observable_organizations.description: Establishes why a subject, problem, or question matters.

observable_organizations.name: Reader-oriented framing
observable_organizations.description: Anticipates what the reader needs to understand before encountering the central claim.

observable_organizations.name: Integrated opening
observable_organizations.description: Coordinates several functions (topic, context, problem, significance, direction) into a coherent beginning.

observable_organizations.name: Deliberately indirect opening
observable_organizations.description: Begins through narrative, image, scene, or conceptual exploration and delays explicit framing for a purposeful reason. Do not assume indirect organization is deficient.

observable_organizations.name: Overloaded opening
observable_organizations.description: Attempts too many functions or introduces too many ideas before a governing purpose becomes clear.

observable_organizations.name: Formula-driven opening
observable_organizations.description: Visibly follows a learned template, but the elements may not yet function together meaningfully.

relationship_notes.Whole Essay Purpose: Interpret the opening in relation to what the whole essay is trying to accomplish.
relationship_notes.Audience Awareness: The opening helps establish what the reader needs in order to enter the essay.
relationship_notes.Central Claim / Thesis: The opening may state, prepare, complicate, or deliberately delay the central claim.
relationship_notes.Organization: The opening establishes expectations for the movement of the essay.
relationship_notes.Paragraph Purpose: An introductory paragraph may perform one or several coordinated functions.
relationship_notes.Word Choice and Voice: The opening often establishes tone, stance, and the writer-reader relationship.
relationship_notes.Revision and Reflective Control: The student's explanation of why an opening changed is evidence of intentional control.

genre_sensitivity.note: Do not apply one introduction model to all genres. Reason from the actual assignment and teacher purpose rather than infer genre solely from surface form.
genre_sensitivity.argumentative: May orient the reader to an issue, establish stakes, frame a problem, and prepare or state a claim.
genre_sensitivity.expository: May define the topic, establish scope, orient the reader, and indicate the organizing purpose.
genre_sensitivity.analytical: May identify an object of analysis, establish a conceptual problem, and prepare an interpretation.
genre_sensitivity.research: May establish context, identify a research problem, define scope, explain significance, and introduce a guiding claim or question.
genre_sensitivity.personal: May establish a voice, situation, experience, or tension without immediately stating an explicit thesis.
genre_sensitivity.narrative: May establish scene, character, conflict, perspective, or narrative expectation.
genre_sensitivity.reflective: May establish an experience, question, uncertainty, or transformation to be explored.
genre_sensitivity.literary_analysis: May introduce the work, establish an interpretive issue, and orient the reader toward a claim.

domains.inside_outside_coordination: Begin by interpreting the organization already present in the student's writing. Distinguish among the student's operative purpose, the assigned purpose, the teacher's pedagogical purpose, the reader's needs, and the cultural resources for openings. A mismatch must not automatically be treated as a student deficit — it may indicate unclear assignment expectations, a different student purpose, a reasonable alternative organization, insufficient reader orientation, an unfinished draft, tension between genre expectations and writer intention, or a need to clarify the immediate task. The next invitation should extend, differentiate, integrate, or productively challenge the student's present organization, not replace it with a conventional formula.
prohibitions: require a hook
require a rhetorical question
require broad-to-narrow organization
require a thesis in the final sentence
require all opening functions to appear
assume every opening is one paragraph
reject an unconventional beginning merely because it is unconventional
evaluate the opening without reference to purpose, audience, genre, and the developing whole
provide a rewritten introduction
provide a polished model introduction for the student to imitate
list every weakness
classify the student into a stage or level
infer a stable writing ability from one introduction
treat the canonical domain as a rubric or grading checklist

cultural_resources.name: Hook
cultural_resources.purpose: Solves the problem of a reader who has no reason yet to care or keep reading.
cultural_resources.functional_definition: A hook is not just a dramatic or surprising sentence. It is an opening move that engages the reader while preparing them for the essay's real concern.
typical_misunderstandings: Every introduction must begin with a hook.
Any shocking or clever sentence is a good hook.
A hook can be unrelated to the essay as long as it grabs attention.
appropriate_uses: When the reader needs a reason to enter the topic.
When engagement and orientation can be combined.
When the genre rewards drawing the reader in (argument, feature, personal).
inappropriate_uses: When a knowledgeable audience needs orientation more than enticement.
When a dramatic opener would distort or misrepresent the essay.
When the genre expects a direct, sober opening (some research/technical writing).

developmental_connections.purpose: engages the reader in service of the essay's purpose
developmental_connections.audience: shaped by what will actually interest this reader
developmental_connections.organization: leads into context and the eventual claim

cultural_resources.student_friendly_explanation: A hook is a way of opening so your reader leans in — not a trick, but a door into what your essay is really about.
cultural_resources.explanation_note: This is a seed. Adapt the wording to the student's current organization, the assignment, the genre, and what the student has already shown they understand. Do not simply recite it.

cultural_resources.name: Significance
cultural_resources.purpose: Solves the problem of a reader who understands the topic but not why it matters.
cultural_resources.functional_definition: Significance is the move that shows what is at stake — why this topic deserves the reader's attention now.
typical_misunderstandings: Saying a topic is 'important' establishes significance.
Significance is the same as background.
appropriate_uses: When the reader may see the topic as obvious or trivial.
When stakes motivate the argument to come.
inappropriate_uses: When stakes are already obvious to this audience.
When asserting importance would substitute for grounding it.

developmental_connections.purpose: connects the topic to why it matters
developmental_connections.audience: what this reader would find at stake

cultural_resources.student_friendly_explanation: Significance is where you show your reader why this is worth their time — not by saying 'this is important' but by making the stakes visible.
cultural_resources.explanation_note: This is a seed. Adapt the wording to the student's current organization, the assignment, the genre, and what the student has already shown they understand. Do not simply recite it.

domain_status.description: Culturally available functions and resources for giving an essay a controlling idea.

domains.governing_communicative_function: Give the essay a controlling idea that organizes its parts and communicates to the reader what the whole essay is trying to establish, interpret, or explore. What counts as a claim, how explicit it must be, and where it appears depend on the essay's purpose and genre.
communicative_functions: make a position or interpretation arguable
possible_communicative_functions: answer a question the essay poses
frame an inquiry or line of exploration
make a claim arguable rather than merely factual
establish the scope of what is claimed
signal the essay's direction and structure
distinguish the writer's claim from common opinion
commit to something a reader could dispute
hold body paragraphs accountable to one idea
synthesize several observations into one governing idea
domains.engine_note_on_functions: Not every genre requires an explicit, early, single-sentence thesis. A claim may be stated, implied, distributed, delayed, or exploratory.
reader_needs: knowing what the essay is trying to establish
being able to tell the claim apart from the topic
understanding what is being asserted, interpreted, or asked
knowing what would count as support
being able to predict the essay's direction
understanding the scope and limits of the claim
seeing why the claim is worth making (arguable, not obvious)
domains.resources_note: Introduce a resource only when it serves the writer's operative purpose and the essay's genre. No single thesis form is required.

observable_organizations.name: Topic without claim
observable_organizations.description: Names a subject but asserts nothing arguable.
observable_organizations.example: This essay is about social media.

observable_organizations.name: Opinion without reasoning
observable_organizations.description: States a like/dislike or 'should' with no grounds.

observable_organizations.name: Factual statement as thesis
observable_organizations.description: An accurate but non-arguable fact stands in for a claim.
observable_organizations.example: The Amazon is the largest rainforest.

observable_organizations.name: Overly broad claim
observable_organizations.description: A claim so large the essay cannot support it.
observable_organizations.example: Technology has changed everything about society.

observable_organizations.name: Vague claim
observable_organizations.description: A claim whose key terms are undefined or fuzzy.
observable_organizations.example: Social media has a big impact on people.

observable_organizations.name: Multiple competing claims
observable_organizations.description: Several candidate claims coexist without one governing them.

observable_organizations.name: Clear but unsupported claim
observable_organizations.description: A sharp, arguable claim with no visible support yet.

observable_organizations.name: Implicit claim
observable_organizations.description: The claim is inferable from the writing but never stated.

observable_organizations.name: Delayed claim
observable_organizations.description: The claim is purposefully withheld until later.

observable_organizations.name: Distributed claim
observable_organizations.description: The claim is spread across several sentences or parts rather than one statement.

observable_organizations.name: Exploratory thesis
observable_organizations.description: The essay frames an inquiry or question it will investigate rather than assert.

observable_organizations.name: Interpretive thesis
observable_organizations.description: Asserts a reading or meaning of an object (text, event, data).

observable_organizations.name: Argumentative thesis
observable_organizations.description: Takes a disputable position and commits to defending it.

observable_organizations.name: Analytical thesis
observable_organizations.description: Claims how or why something works, or what it reveals.

observable_organizations.name: Research question in place of a thesis
observable_organizations.description: Organized by a question the essay answers.

observable_organizations.name: Formulaic three-part thesis
observable_organizations.description: 'X because A, B, and C' template; the parts may not cohere.

observable_organizations.name: Integrated / coordinated claim
observable_organizations.description: A claim that governs the body and is answerable to it.

observable_organizations.name: Claim mismatched to assignment
observable_organizations.description: A real claim that does not address what was assigned.

observable_organizations.name: Claim mismatched to body
observable_organizations.description: The stated claim and what the essay actually argues diverge.

relationship_notes.Whole Essay Purpose: The claim is the controlling idea through which the whole purpose is realized.
relationship_notes.Opening / Introduction: The opening may state, prepare, complicate, or deliberately delay the claim.
relationship_notes.Paragraph Purpose: Each paragraph should be answerable to the claim.
relationship_notes.Evidence: A claim defines what would count as support.
relationship_notes.Interpretation / Reasoning: Reasoning connects evidence to the claim and makes it defensible.
relationship_notes.Organization: The claim sets expectations for how the essay proceeds.
relationship_notes.Conclusion: The conclusion may return to, extend, or qualify the claim.
relationship_notes.Revision and Reflective Control: Explaining why a claim changed is evidence of intentional control.

genre_sensitivity.note: Do not apply one thesis model to all genres. Reason from the actual assignment and teacher purpose rather than infer genre solely from surface form.
genre_sensitivity.argumentative: Usually commits to a disputable position the essay defends; may state it early or build to it.
genre_sensitivity.expository: May use an organizing or controlling idea, or a thesis of scope, rather than a contested claim.
genre_sensitivity.analytical: Asserts how or why something works, or what an object means; interpretive rather than merely factual.
genre_sensitivity.research: May be a guiding claim OR a research question/hypothesis the study investigates.
genre_sensitivity.personal: May have no explicit thesis; a controlling insight or tension may organize instead.
genre_sensitivity.narrative: Typically organized by event and meaning, not an explicit thesis; do not force one.
genre_sensitivity.reflective: May be organized by a question, uncertainty, or evolving understanding rather than a fixed claim.
genre_sensitivity.literary_analysis: Advances an interpretive claim about the text, supported by textual evidence.

domains.inside_outside_coordination: Begin by interpreting the claim organization already present. Distinguish the student's operative claim, the assigned purpose, the teacher's pedagogical purpose, the reader's needs, and the genre's conventions for claims. A missing or unconventional thesis is not automatically a deficit — it may reflect a genre that does not require one, a purposeful delay, an exploratory design, an unfinished draft, or a mismatch between the assignment and the writer's intention. The next invitation should help the student differentiate, scope, consolidate, make explicit, or align the claim — never supply the claim itself.

require the thesis in the final sentence of the introduction
require the 'X because A, B, and C' form
treat a factual statement as automatically acceptable or unacceptable without reference to purpose
reject a question-driven or exploratory thesis merely because it is not a statement
force a personal or narrative essay to state an argumentative thesis
evaluate the claim in isolation from purpose, audience, genre, evidence, and the body
write or rewrite the student's thesis
provide a polished model thesis for the student to copy
list every weakness of the claim
classify the student into a stage, level, or ability
infer a stable writing ability from one thesis
treat the domain as a grading rubric or checklist

cultural_resources.name: Thesis
cultural_resources.purpose: Solves the problem of an essay whose parts do not add up to one governing idea.
cultural_resources.functional_definition: A thesis is not merely an opinion. It is the controlling idea that gives an essay direction and holds its parts accountable to one purpose.
typical_misunderstandings: A thesis must be one sentence at the end of the first paragraph.
A thesis must follow 'X because A, B, and C.'
A fact can be a thesis.
Every genre needs an explicit thesis.
appropriate_uses: When the essay needs a controlling idea to organize its parts.
When the reader must know what the essay will establish.
inappropriate_uses: When the genre organizes by question, narrative, or reflection instead.
When forcing an early explicit claim would flatten purposeful inquiry.

developmental_connections.purpose: the idea through which the whole purpose is realized
developmental_connections.organization: sets expectations for the essay's movement

cultural_resources.student_friendly_explanation: A thesis is the one idea your whole essay is trying to get a reader to accept, understand, or see differently — the spine everything else hangs on.
cultural_resources.explanation_note: This is a seed. Adapt the wording to the student's current organization, the assignment, the genre, and what the student has already shown they understand. Do not simply recite it.

cultural_resources.name: Claim
cultural_resources.purpose: Solves the problem of writing that reports or opines without asserting anything a reader could reasonably dispute.
cultural_resources.functional_definition: A claim is a statement you take a position on and could defend — not a fact and not a bare preference.
typical_misunderstandings: An opinion is automatically a claim.
A true statement is a strong claim.
appropriate_uses: When the assignment asks you to argue or interpret.
When you want the reader to accept something contestable.
inappropriate_uses: When the task is purely to explain or narrate.
When the 'claim' is really just a topic.

developmental_connections.evidence: a claim tells you what to support

cultural_resources.student_friendly_explanation: A claim is something a thoughtful person could disagree with — that's what makes it worth arguing and gives your evidence a job.

domain_status.description: Culturally available functions and resources for the work a paragraph does within a whole essay.
is_not: a rule that every paragraph opens with a topic sentence
a rule that every paragraph must be claim-evidence-analysis
a rule that a paragraph performs only one function
the same thing as the paragraph's topic
must_be_interpreted_relative_to: the central claim or controlling idea
the organization of the developing whole essay

domains.governing_communicative_function: A paragraph is a locally organized movement of meaning that performs one or more coordinated functions in relation to the developing whole text. Its purpose is the work it does for the reader and the essay, not merely the topic it names.
communicative_functions: do a definable job for the essay
organize sentences under one local movement
domains.engine_note_on_functions: This is not a checklist or fixed taxonomy. A paragraph may perform one function or several coordinated functions. Do not require any particular function.
reader_needs: knowing what this paragraph is doing for the argument or essay
seeing how the paragraph connects to the one before it
understanding why this paragraph appears here
being able to follow one local movement without confusion
knowing which idea governs the sentences
seeing the paragraph's contribution to the whole
canonical_writing_resources: descriptive detail in service of a point
domains.resources_note: Introduce a resource only when it serves the paragraph's function, the genre, and the reader. No single paragraph structure is required.

observable_organizations.name: Topic without purpose
observable_organizations.description: Names a subject for the paragraph but does no definable work for the essay.
observable_organizations.example: There are many things about pollution.

observable_organizations.name: Clear purpose, disconnected from whole
observable_organizations.description: The paragraph does a clear local job but its relation to the thesis/essay is not visible.

observable_organizations.name: Competing purposes
observable_organizations.description: Several distinct jobs coexist in one paragraph without a governing movement.

observable_organizations.name: Purpose shift midway
observable_organizations.description: The paragraph begins doing one job and silently switches to another.

observable_organizations.name: Clear function, no explicit topic sentence
observable_organizations.description: The paragraph clearly does a job though no single sentence announces it (may be inductive/narrative).

observable_organizations.name: Topic sentence that does not govern
observable_organizations.description: A formulaic opening sentence is present but the rest of the paragraph does not follow from it.

observable_organizations.name: Evidence without interpretation
observable_organizations.description: Facts/quotations are supplied but their meaning for the claim is not made.

observable_organizations.name: Interpretation without sufficient evidence
observable_organizations.description: Claims about meaning are asserted without grounding.

observable_organizations.name: Necessary context
observable_organizations.description: The paragraph orients the reader with background the essay genuinely needs.

observable_organizations.name: Overloaded with unnecessary background
observable_organizations.description: Background exceeds what the reader needs and delays the essay's movement.

observable_organizations.name: Develops the central claim
observable_organizations.description: The paragraph advances or extends the thesis with new work.

observable_organizations.name: Repeats the thesis without developing
observable_organizations.description: Restates the controlling idea but adds no development.

observable_organizations.name: Complicates or qualifies the thesis
observable_organizations.description: Introduces tension, limitation, or nuance to the claim.

observable_organizations.name: Acknowledges another perspective
observable_organizations.description: Represents a view other than the writer's.

observable_organizations.name: Responds to an objection
observable_organizations.description: Answers a counter-position or anticipated challenge.

observable_organizations.name: Transitional / bridge
observable_organizations.description: Chiefly connects sections or movements rather than developing content.

observable_organizations.name: Narrative paragraph
observable_organizations.description: Organized as an event sequence; should not be forced into claim-evidence-analysis.

observable_organizations.name: Reflective paragraph around uncertainty
observable_organizations.description: Organized by a question or unresolved thinking rather than a settled point.

observable_organizations.name: Descriptive serving analysis
observable_organizations.description: Description whose purpose is to enable a larger analytical point.

observable_organizations.name: Dependent on neighbor
observable_organizations.description: Only coheres when read with the preceding or following paragraph (part of a multi-paragraph movement).

observable_organizations.name: Integrated multi-function movement
observable_organizations.description: Coordinates several functions (e.g., concede -> rebut -> extend) into one coherent movement.

observable_organizations.name: Mismatch with assignment
observable_organizations.description: A competent paragraph whose apparent weakness is that it does not serve what was assigned.

domains.observable_organizations_note: Descriptive organizations, not stages and not exhaustive. Multiple readings may fit; look for evidence before deciding.
possible_differentiations: the paragraph's local job from its relation to the whole
development of a claim from repetition of a claim
a governing idea from a decorative opening sentence
one integrated movement from several competing jobs
a deliberately inductive build from an ungoverned paragraph
possible_integrations: paragraph purpose with the central claim
evidence with its interpretation
concession with rebuttal
context with the point it enables
description with the analysis it serves
the paragraph with the preceding paragraph's movement
the paragraph with the following paragraph it sets up
several sentences under one governing idea
several functions into one coherent movement
possible_coordinations: the assignment and what the paragraph is doing
the thesis and each paragraph's job
the paragraph and its neighbors
evidence and reasoning within the paragraph
audience needs and the paragraph's orientation
the paragraph's function and the essay's overall organization
local movement and global progression
genre expectations and paragraph form
common_productive_tensions: A topic is named but the paragraph does no definable work.
The paragraph does a clear job but its link to the thesis is invisible.
Several purposes compete and none governs the paragraph.
The paragraph shifts purpose midway without signaling it.
A function is clearly performed but no sentence states it, and it is unclear whether that is purposeful.
A topic sentence is present but does not govern the paragraph.
Evidence is present but its meaning for the claim is not made.
Interpretation is asserted without enough evidence.
Context is useful but exceeds what the reader needs.
The paragraph restates the thesis without developing it.
The paragraph complicates the claim, but the relation to the main argument is unclear.
A counter-perspective is raised but not yet answered or positioned.
A transitional paragraph connects but its own contribution is thin.
A narrative paragraph is being pushed toward argument it need not make.
The paragraph only coheres with a neighbor, and that dependence is not yet coordinated.
The paragraph is competent but does not serve the assignment.
Multiple functions are present and it is unclear whether they are integrated or overloaded.
domains.tensions_note: Identify only ONE primary tension at a time.

domains.alternative_interpretations_note: Do not assume one interpretation without evidence; preserve plausible alternatives.
common_misunderstandings: Every paragraph must begin with a topic sentence.
The topic sentence must always be the first sentence.
Every paragraph must follow claim-evidence-analysis.
A paragraph can perform only one function.
Paragraph purpose is the same as paragraph topic.
A paragraph can be evaluated in isolation from its neighbors.
Longer paragraphs are automatically more developed.
A narrative or reflective paragraph is deficient if it lacks a claim.
Restating the thesis counts as developing it.
A transition sentence at the end is enough to connect paragraphs.
More background is always more helpful to the reader.
domains.misunderstandings_note: Be alert to these but do not automatically assume them.

from an isolated paragraph to one coordinated with the whole essay
from competing purposes to one governing movement
from a purpose shift to a deliberate, signaled progression
from evidence alone to evidence plus interpretation
from asserted interpretation to grounded interpretation
from repeating the thesis to developing it
from an ungoverned paragraph to a clearly governed one (topic sentence OR coherent inductive build)
from raising a counter-view to positioning or answering it
from a paragraph read in isolation to one coordinated with its neighbors
from content-focus to function-awareness (what the paragraph is doing)
from a genre-mismatched form to a form that fits the paragraph's job
domains.movements_note: Possible reorganizations, not a required progression.
candidate_developmental_invitations: state, in a few words, the one job this paragraph is doing for the essay
distinguish what this paragraph is about (topic) from what it is trying to do (purpose)
explain how this paragraph connects to the paragraph before it
identify which sentence, if any, governs the paragraph
decide which of the competing jobs should govern the paragraph
point to where the paragraph shifts purpose and decide whether to split it
explain what a specific piece of evidence shows about your claim
identify what evidence would ground the interpretation you are making
decide how much of this background the reader actually needs
explain how this paragraph develops the thesis rather than repeating it
position the perspective you raised: do you concede, answer, or extend it?
explain what this paragraph sets up in the paragraph that follows
test whether this paragraph still makes sense if the neighboring paragraph were removed
explain what changed about the paragraph's job after your revision
domains.invitations_note: Invitations should require the student to think, explain, choose, or revise. Present only one at a time.

three_parts: Brief recognition of an observable feature in the student's paragraph
Connection to the current communicative purpose or the whole essay
One intellectual or writing action for the student to perform
invitation_construction_rules.example_form: This paragraph gives the reader several facts about the recycling center. To help the reader see why they are here, try saying in a phrase what job this paragraph is doing for your argument.
cautions: Do not use the example as a fixed verbal template.
Do not rewrite the paragraph for the student.

relationship_notes.Whole Essay Purpose: A paragraph's job is defined by what the whole essay is trying to do.
relationship_notes.Central Claim / Thesis: Most body paragraphs should be answerable to the controlling idea.
relationship_notes.Organization: Paragraph purpose is realized through where the paragraph sits in the essay's movement.
relationship_notes.Evidence: A paragraph that presents evidence coordinates with how that evidence supports the claim.
relationship_notes.Interpretation / Reasoning: Interpreting evidence is often the work a paragraph must do.
relationship_notes.Transitions: Connections between paragraphs make a paragraph's relation to its neighbors explicit.
relationship_notes.Opening / Introduction: An introductory paragraph may perform one or several coordinated opening functions.
relationship_notes.Revision and Reflective Control: Explaining why a paragraph's job changed is evidence of intentional control.

genre_sensitivity.note: Do not apply one paragraph model to all genres. Reason from the actual assignment and teacher purpose rather than infer genre solely from surface form.
genre_sensitivity.argumentative: Body paragraphs typically develop, support, complicate, or defend the claim; forms vary.
genre_sensitivity.expository: Paragraphs may define, explain, exemplify, or sequence information toward the organizing idea.
genre_sensitivity.analytical: Paragraphs often move between evidence and interpretation to build an analysis.
genre_sensitivity.research: Paragraphs may report, synthesize sources, or situate findings; some are chiefly contextual.
genre_sensitivity.personal: Paragraphs may narrate, reflect, or dwell; a stated point is not required.
genre_sensitivity.narrative: Paragraphs advance scene, action, or meaning; do not force claim-evidence-analysis.
genre_sensitivity.reflective: Paragraphs may be organized around questions or evolving understanding.
genre_sensitivity.literary_analysis: Paragraphs typically coordinate textual evidence with interpretive claims.

domains.inside_outside_coordination: Begin by interpreting what the paragraph is already doing and how it sits among its neighbors. Distinguish the student's operative purpose, the assigned purpose, the teacher's pedagogical purpose, the reader's needs, the genre, and the paragraph's relation to the whole. A missing topic sentence, multiple functions, or a loose connection is not automatically a deficit — it may be inductive, narrative, transitional, part of a multi-paragraph movement, or an unfinished draft. The next invitation should help the student clarify, differentiate, or coordinate the paragraph's job — never supply the paragraph.
prohibitions: require a topic sentence in every paragraph
require the topic sentence to be the first sentence
require claim-evidence-analysis in every genre or every paragraph
assume a paragraph can perform only one function
treat paragraph purpose as identical to paragraph topic
evaluate a paragraph in isolation from its neighbors and the whole
force a narrative or reflective paragraph into an argumentative structure
write or rewrite the student's paragraph
provide a polished model paragraph for the student to copy
list every weakness of the paragraph
classify the student into a stage, level, or ability
infer a stable writing ability from one paragraph
treat the domain as a grading rubric or checklist

cultural_resources.name: Topic Sentence
cultural_resources.purpose: Solves the problem of a paragraph whose sentences do not obviously belong together or serve the essay.
cultural_resources.functional_definition: A topic sentence names the job a paragraph is doing so the reader can follow one local movement. It need not be the first sentence, and some paragraphs (inductive, narrative) govern themselves differently.
typical_misunderstandings: Every paragraph must open with a topic sentence.
The topic sentence must be the first sentence.
A topic sentence is the paragraph's topic.
appropriate_uses: When a paragraph's job would otherwise be unclear.
When the reader needs a signpost for the local movement.
inappropriate_uses: When the paragraph is deliberately inductive or narrative.
When a stated sentence would spoil a built effect.
When it merely names a topic instead of a purpose.
cultural_resources.student_friendly_explanation: A topic sentence is a quick signpost telling your reader what this paragraph is doing — it can go anywhere, and some paragraphs earn their point instead of announcing it.
cultural_resources.explanation_note: This is a seed. Adapt the wording to the student's current organization, the assignment, the genre, and what the student has already shown they understand. Do not simply recite it.

cultural_resources.name: Transition
cultural_resources.purpose: Solves the problem of paragraphs that sit next to each other without a visible relationship.
cultural_resources.functional_definition: A transition makes the relationship between ideas explicit — it signals a conceptual move (contrast, cause, extension), not just a verbal connector.
typical_misunderstandings: A transition is just a word like 'however' or 'furthermore.'
Transitions only go at the start of paragraphs.
appropriate_uses: When the logical relationship between parts is not obvious.
When a section shifts and the reader needs to know why.
inappropriate_uses: When the connection is already clear.
When a connective word is used to fake a link that isn't there.
cultural_resources.student_friendly_explanation: A transition is where you tell your reader how one idea relates to the next — a real bridge in meaning, not just a word like 'however.'
cultural_resources.explanation_note: This is a seed. Adapt the wording to the student's current organization, the assignment, the genre, and what the student has already shown they understand. Do not simply recite it.

coordinating evidence with interpretation

evidence present but its relevance is unstated

making the warrant explicit

Does the organization support the purpose?

possible_integrations: subordinating parts to a whole structure
aligning order with purpose
common_productive_tensions: ideas are present but their order is arbitrary

candidate_developmental_invitations: ask why one part comes before another
